4	\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
5	\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursively training language models on their own outputs erodes distributional tails, eventually collapsing the output distribution to a narrow mode.

7	The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this analysis to self-consuming generative models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff as synthetic data accumulates across generations.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Web-crawled training corpora are accumulating synthetic text at an accelerating rate.
As deployed language models generate text that is published, re-crawled, and used to train the next generation of models, recursive model$\to$data$\to$model feedback loops emerge with no explicit orchestration \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
The consequences of this recursion depend critically on its depth: first-generation synthetic data can supplement training corpora without measurable degradation \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate}, but deeply recursive text drives distributional collapse---eroding tail coverage, compressing lexical diversity, and narrowing the effective support of the output distribution \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails,marchi2024_heat_death}.
A data curator deciding what to keep, downweight, or discard therefore needs more than a binary real-versus-synthetic label; the relevant question is \emph{how many recursive cycles a text has undergone}.

No existing method answers this question.
Binary detectors---Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}---classify text as human-written or machine-generated but discard ordinal depth information entirely.
Model collapse studies characterize how recursive training degrades output distributions, yet treat generation depth as a known experimental variable rather than a quantity to be inferred \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the extent of single-pass AI editing but does not model multi-step recursive chains.
Detection-based filtering can slow collapse \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}, but only if the filter can distinguish shallow from deep recursion---precisely the capability that current tools lack.
The result is a blind spot: the very feedback loops that theory predicts will degrade model quality cannot be diagnosed from the data they produce.

We address this gap by formalizing \textbf{recursive generation depth estimation} as an ordinal classification task and providing the first systematic empirical study of how recursive depth manifests in text statistics.
The core observation is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in reference-model perplexity distributions.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\texttt{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\texttt{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators: \texttt{p90\_ppl} ranks among the top-2 features in all 9 model--strategy configurations we test, and \texttt{var\_surprisal} does so in 7 of 9.
This consistency holds across three model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and three decoding strategies (nucleus, temperature, top-$k$), suggesting that recursive generation compresses the perplexity distribution in a manner that is largely independent of the generating model and sampling method.

Building on this observation, we extract a 19-dimensional feature vector from token-level perplexity distributions computed by a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M) and train ordinal classifiers to predict depth $d \in \{0,1,2,3\}$.
Random Forest classifiers achieve 70--85\% four-class accuracy across the $3 \times 3$ grid (chance level: 25\%), with the strongest configuration (OLMo, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$) reaching 85.4\%.
Notably, these feature-based classifiers substantially outperform end-to-end fine-tuned language models: both DeBERTa-v3-base (58.3\%) and RoBERTa-base (59.5\%) fall well short of the Random Forest (78.2\%), an architecture-independent result that indicates the depth signal resides in distributional statistics that pretrained representations do not readily capture (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).

The paper makes four contributions:

\paragraph{C1: Task formalization.}
We define recursive generation depth estimation, formalize the Effective Discriminable Depth (EDD)---the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain statistically separable (\S\ref{sec:method:edd})---and construct a multi-generational benchmark of 180K samples spanning 3 model families $\times$ 3 decoding strategies $\times$ 4 depths (\S\ref{sec:method}).

\paragraph{C2: Depth Degradation Atlas.}
We provide a systematic empirical map of how 19 statistical features evolve across recursive depths, models, and strategies (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
The Atlas reveals (a)~the universality of \texttt{p90\_ppl} and \texttt{var\_surprisal} as depth markers, (b)~strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal but preserves its direction---and (c)~an EDD boundary: pairwise AUC for adjacent depths $d_3$-vs-$d_4$ clusters near 0.75 across all three models (0.750--0.784), while $d_4$-vs-$d_5$ uniformly falls below 0.70 (0.681--0.694).

\paragraph{C3: Generalization analysis.}
Cross-model leave-one-out evaluation yields 66.4\% mean accuracy, and cross-strategy leave-one-out yields 59.1\% (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
Both substantially exceed chance, but cross-strategy transfer exposes a fundamental asymmetry: temperature sampling induces a structural distributional shift in which depth-$N$ features under temperature approximate depth-$(N{+}1)$ features under nucleus and top-$k$, causing the $d_1$-vs-$d_2$ decision boundary to invert.
This is not a correctable scale artifact---$z$-score normalization does not recover pairwise $d_1$-vs-$d_2$ AUC---but rather a geometry-level shift in feature space that reflects how decoding strategies reshape the degradation trajectory itself.

\paragraph{C4: Negative results on end-to-end learning.}
Six iterations of contrastive ordinal loss (DCOL) across two pretrained backbones (DeBERTa, RoBERTa) fail to match feature-based methods, with failure modes spanning embedding collapse, gradient instability, and catastrophic forgetting (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Combined with the architecture-independent end-to-end baseline results, this establishes that statistical features capture depth information that current discriminative fine-tuning does not extract from raw text.
